newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin passes first cohabitation test with honours.
newsitem.headline: Jospin passes first cohabitation test with honours.

text.p: What is pink, red and green, has no elephants but lots of women? France's new left-wing government.
Analysts said on Thursday that Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin had passed his first test of "cohabitation" with conservative President Jacques Chirac with first-class honours.

By appointing a young, bright, more feminine and tighter cabinet, brimming with new faces, Jospin has given the left an image of innovation and boldness which his Gaullist predecessor, Alain Juppe, tried but failed to do for the right.

While giving jobs to the anti-Maastricht Communists and Citizens' Movement and to the ecologist Greens, he ensured the key cabinet posts are in the hands of pro-European Socialists, including Martine Aubry, his number two and superminister for employment and social solidarity.
In a left-handed compliment to a left-wing administration, the Paris bourse jumped 2.9 percent on Thursday as traders digested the appointment of an economic team seen as reassuring.

Economists said Finance and Industry Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn was regarded as a safe pair of hands, and the Socialists' less strict attitude towards the conditions for a single European currency could favour stronger economic growth.

Jospin has also shown due deference to Chirac in the key areas of foreign affairs and defence, over which the president has a big say under the constitution, by appointing ministers whom the Gaullist head of state should find cooperative.

Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine, a former chief-of-staff to the late president Francois Mitterrand, is a veteran of two past eras of power-sharing and a skilled exponent of France's foreign policy. Defence Minister Alain Richard is a budget expert likely to concentrate on cost-cutting rather than strategic policy.

"Jospin kept his word. He wanted a tight, feminine, plural government with a majority of new faces, and he did it," said political commentator Michele Cotta. "And he did it briskly, without agitation or grandstanding."

But she said Jospin may have made enemies in the Socialist party by shutting out the so-called "elephants", senior figures who were the pillars of Mitterrand's governments and led the party's warring factions.
Among the party barons who got nothing were former culture minister Jack Lang, ex-prime minister Michel Rocard and former Mitterrand ministers Paul Quiles and Pierre Joxe.

Former Socialist prime minister Laurent Fabius, long Jospin's most bitter factional rival, received the prestigious post of president of the National Assembly, which he may find easier than serving under Jospin.
But his faction is poorly represented in the new cabinet. Socialist sources said Claude Bartolone, Fabius' right-hand man, refused to serve under Aubry as secretary of state for health.
Analysts also noted the skill with which Jospin had played off the different components of his rainbow coalition.

Ecologist Greens party leader Dominique Voynet, given a big environment and regional development ministry, will have to lock horns with Communist Transport and Infrastructure Minister Jean-Claude Gayssot on issues such as the disputed Rhine-Rhone canal project, motorway building and road traffic restrictions to combat air pollution.

Gayssot, a former railway technician, will have to manage two of the most strike-prone French public companies, the SNCF railways and flag carrier Air France, which the previous centre-right government had planned to privatise in the face of mounting EU-driven competition.

Anti-Maastricht Citizens' Movement leftist Jean-Pierre Chevenement will have little say in European policy, except to implement closer police cooperation with France's EU partners in the fight against terrorism and drugs trafficking.

He will also be responsible for replacing immigration and nationality laws enacted by his right-wing predecessors which the left has promised to abrogate, even though polls showed they were popular with the electorate.

Jospin's next tests will be how he manages the Socialists' campaign promises to ease the conditions for joining the single European currency and translate pledges of shorter working hours and job-creation into policy without blowing up the budget.
Judging by his first steps in office, he will take his time and seek consensus rather than confrontation.
